subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of the conference in Bermuda. Would he say whether or not discussions took place relative to the European common market and its effect on Canadian trade, and the nature of those discussions, and in particular will he assure us that the results will not be discriminatory to Canadian trade?
Would he also say whether or not, when discussing matters of commonwealth interest, he extended an invitation to the Prime Minister of Great Britain or suggested the convening of a British commonwealth and empire trade conference to the end that our trade areas may be extended and that lost trade may be retrieved?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the first question dealing with the common market, there was a long and most interesting and I hope fruitful discussion with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the Foreign Secretary about the common market and the proposal that the United Kingdom might participate or be associated in some way with that common market arrangement which is being set up, as my hon. friend knows, by six western European countries.
We discussed also the other related suggestion that there might be uniform tariffs within even a larger area of European countries with which the United Kingdom might also be associated.
As we had reason to expect, we found that such anxieties as we had about the possibilities of this common market and the uniform tariff arrangements were anxieties that were very present in the minds of the Prime Minister and the Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom. We found that they shared our own view that this common market with a reasonably low tariff wall around it could be most helpful in promoting further multilateral trade throughout the world because it would enable a larger market to be available for the manufactured products of any one of the countries and

Inquiries of the Ministry thereby would be apt to bring about a reduction in their costs with the greater possibility of those countries selling products outside the common market.
However, it was felt that a very different situation might be created if instead of having this common market designed to increase the economic strength and the ability of these countries to trade with the rest of the world it was designed to be a closed market with a tariff wall around it which would prevent other countries from trading with the common market area. The United Kingdom authorities felt that there was little likelihood of that latter alternative being the one resorted to and in that way confirmed the view which the premier of France had expressed when we had similar talks with him during the course of his visit to Ottawa. I say again that we were not surprised but happily confirmed in our impression that the United Kingdom would have about the same anxieties we had. As they are participants in the negotiations we felt that those anxieties would be voiced there and would receive consideration.
As far as the United Kingdom is concerned, this would not apply to raw materials, foodstuffs or like things. We hope it could be established and implemented in a fashion which would strengthen the economies of the participating nations and make it easier for them to do away more rapidly with the present restrictions which exist against multilateral trade generally.
With respect to the second part of the hon. gentleman's question, it was not necessary to issue any invitation. I found that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom had actively in mind the advisability of having a conference of prime ministers at a relatively early date.

subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: A trade and economic conference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
There was no discussion about a trade and economic conference. We were satisfied from our talks, by the degree to which there had been an improvement over the last calendar year both in our imports from the United Kingdom and our exports to the United Kingdom, that much had been done. We pointed out to the United Kingdom some small matters that were inconvenient, and which would not be apt to affect in any serious way their balance of payments, and which would help to maintain and increase the cordiality of the trading relations between our two countries; and note was taken of those matters.
I do not know if this has been publicly announced, but there is to be a meeting of


the permanent Anglo-Canadian committee on trade questions here in Ottawa during the month of May. The committee is to meet here in Ottawa for one of its periodical meetings and, as I say, notes were taken on the matters to which their attention is to be called, so that the officials may be properly briefed in relation to these matters, and prepared to discuss them, and to discuss their possible advantageous or disadvantageous repercussions.
With respect to the meeting of the prime ministers, I found that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom felt quite strongly that on this occasion the meeting should again be held in London, but that we should at that meeting arrange for a system of holding some of these meetings in other countries of the commonwealth.

subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that the prime ministers' conference should be held in various parts of the commonwealth would naturally meet with the support of Canadians and, I am sure, of members of the other nations of the commonwealth. It should be encouraged.
However, returning to this question of trade, did the Prime Minister not consider, the opportunity being there, that an invitation should be extended not only to the United Kingdom but to all the other parts of the commonwealth to take part in a trade conference in order to build up our trade with other parts of the commonwealth, and to consolidate and expand trade relations which today are being challenged by the U.S.S.R. and communism in general? Did the Prime Minister not bring up at all the question of a trade and economic conference?

subtopic: BERMUDA MEETING
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I did not. We discussed trade relations between Canada and the United Kingdom and the matters which it would be desirable to have this permanent joint committee of officials consider at its next meeting which is to take place here in Ottawa during the month of May.

subtopic: ARMED SERVICES
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ELIGIBILITY OF MEMBERS
speechtext:
On Friday, March 22, the hon. member for Peterborough, as reported at page 2593 of Hansard, asked whether it is true that a man who has been in the armed services for three years is entitled to unemployment insurance but is not entitled if he signs for a further period. I said then that involved in that question was whether or not the man who serves in the armed forces had or had not served in a theatre of action. I asked my hon. friend whether, if he had a special case in mind, he would let me have the details and he very kindly sent me the details of the case.
In reply to this question, I may say it is true that no unemployment insurance contributions are payable by the Department of Veterans Affairs on behalf of a veteran who enlisted between July 5, 1950, and July 1, 1955, and who served more than three years unless part of that service was in a theatre of operations, for example, in Korea. It follows that unemployment insurance benefits could not be paid for such service. Service in the armed forces is not an insured employment under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Provision is made, however, in the


Veterans Benefit Act, which is administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs, for the payment of contributions in respect of certain categories of veterans having shortterm engagements.
Specifically, this matter is covered in section 12 of the Veterans Benefit Act, and for the veteran whose name my hon. friend has given to me it is set out in subparagraph 2 (d) of section 12.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. subtopic: ONTARIO
subsubtopic: FLUE-CURED TOBACCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps in view of the fact that my previous answers have not appeared to register upon my hon. friend I had better briefly review this matter and bring into relation with one another the various parts of it.
It will be recalled that when the combines report was published on the Ontario flue-cured tobacco marketing association in November last I said I was confident the association, after carefully reading the report, would review its own arrangements in the light of the report's recommendations; and that we in the department would review the matter after the expiration of a reasonable time.
It has now become apparent that the association has reviewed its position in the light of the report which was made concerning it, and that a move has been announced and made by some of the members of the association to come under provincial marketing legislation. In connection with that move a vote is being taken by the farm products marketing board of Ontario on April 1 next.

It seems to me since that vote is being taken under provincial marketing legislation, which I am sure my hon. friend as a former crown prosecutor would agree, is provincial legislation it should follow therefore that any impropriety in the matter of influencing the vote and the like that might take place in connection with the vote is a matter to be dealt with entirely by the provincial authorities.
I know that this matter has excited a great deal of interest. The hon. members for Norfolk (Mr. Anderson), for Kent, Ont. (Mr. Huffman), and for Essex South (Mr. Clark) have discussed it with me almost daily during the last week. But our federal authority in the matter is confined entirely to the administration of the Combines Investigation Act and all the matters that arise in connection with the taking of votes under provincial marketing legislation are those for which the provincial authorities are responsible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I was about half through the speech which I started last Friday afternoon when I was interrupted by the private bills hour starting at five o'clock. At that time I had reached the point in my speech where I was referring to the announcement by the Minister of National Revenue that the dividend which the Alberta government proposed to pay to its citizens by reason of oil royalties would be taxable for income tax purposes.
I had said that I was rather surprised that the Minister of National Revenue had not adopted a little different attitude when replying to several questions which had been asked on the matter and indicate that he would be willing to receive representations from the Alberta government or even from taxpayers as to whether or not such dividends should be taxable under the Income Tax Act. I was disappointed that the minister was somewhat hasty although he said that his officials had looked into the matter. I felt that he should have taken the attitude that even if he thought those dividends were taxable
[Mr. Barnett.)
the tax on them would not be collected for a year anyway, which would give plenty of time for the Alberta government or other interested parties to make representations.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, may I say to the hon. gentleman that my answer was in response to a question asked by an hon. member from Alberta and you cannot defer for a year the answering of a question. We will be glad to receive representations from anybody in connection with this matter. Probably an official representation is being made now by a resident of Alberta and if it is it will be taken into consideration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was quite prepared to have the minister jump up any moment and attempt an explanation because I saw him in his seat. Of course I will take his remarks for what they are worth. Several hon. members have asked questions on this matter and I was particularly interested in the question asked by my leader on March 8, as reported on page 2008 of Hansard. The question was as follows:
I should like to put a question, to the hon. Minister of National Revenue arising out of some questions that were asked yesterday. Will the minister, until he has given the whole matter full and earnest study, keep an open mind on the subject of whether the dividends announced by the Alberta government last week are to be considered as taxable income and, rather than prejudge the matter, will he carefully consider that this dividend might be a return of capital or, possibly, be in the same class as certain co-operative payments to shareholders that are free from income tax?
I shall not take the time to read all of the minister's reply, but the pertinent part was as follows:
As I said, this is highly technical; the basis of payment will have to be determined upon review of the provincial legislation or regulation authorizing payment. As yet, we have no copies of the legislation, but the matter will be considered when that information has been received.
We were quite prepared to accept that answer made on March 8, but on March 18 the minister gave another answer, as reported on page 2398 of Hansard, as follows:
Taxability:	It is the opinion of officials of my
department that these dividends are income and taxable as such under the Income Tax Act.
There you have it. I was simply indicating to the minister that he should not be in too much of a rush. I wonder if the minister asked the Alberta government whether they would have anything to say in case the decision was what the minister declared it to be? I do not think I am straining at a gnat, but it does occur to me that the government wants to get their fingers into the pot. I should not say "pot" because in the past the Social Credit proposals have been pictured in cartoons and jest as being pie in the sky. If

they are pie in the sky then it seems to me that this centralized and powerful government is trying to dip their fingers into the pie.
If these dividends are to be taxable under the Income Tax Act then I suggest that this government are putting their fingers into the pie to the tune of about $2 million. That figure may not be exact, but I calculate it on the basis of the average income of those who will receive this yearly dividend from Alberta as being in one of the lowest brackets. Referring to the T form I find that the tax on a taxable income of $1,000 is $150 plus 17 per cent on the next $1,000. I think I am reasonable in calculating that the average taxable income will be in the range of $1,000 to $2,000. That being so 17 per cent of the dividends will be collected by this government in the form of income tax, and if my calculation is correct that would amount to around $2 million.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us go a little further. It is quite possible that this dividend being received by the people will be regarded by them as just a little extra windfall, not too much, $22 per person. And they may immediately say: It is pretty nice to have that extra money that we have been needing to buy shoes for the youngsters. Or, maybe, the wife will be able to buy a new dress. Perhaps something may be needed for the home. In other words, I suggest that most of it, coming in the way it does, will be spent by the citizens of Alberta; and when they spend it, this government will also receive the sales tax on that whole amount -not less than 10 per cent.
And if some of the citizens say we can have a little extra liquor, or we can spend it on smokes or on something that carries an excise tax in addition to the sales tax, then the government will be receiving still further revenue on that money. Once again I want to say that the job of the Minister of National Revenue is to collect taxes. I would not want his job because it is a thankless one. And after he has been in the same job for a number of years he gets "tough". I think that at heart he is a tenderhearted man, but when it comes to tax collection he likes to receive the honours, and the honours from his government depend on how much he has been able to collect-how much he has been able to squeeze out of the people. He glories in the fact that he has been able to collect every penny piece; and he is going to get every penny piece out of this extra money that is coming to the people of Alberta by reason of the fact that the natural resources belong to the people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do want to say a word about the nature of this dividend, because when this was first announced the
The Budget-Mr. Hansell newspapers and the politicians said this was a far cry from the dividend of $25 a month which was promised the people of Alberta in 1935. Now I will not take time to go into the implications of that $25 a month. As a matter of fact I was on the ground at the time, and took some part in those pre-election days when Social Credit was first proposed to the people. I know something about those proposals and I doubt very much whether that $25 was actually promised to the people. The fact of the matter is that we were talking in terms of a national dividend and the fact that in the ordinary process of the economic system there was never enough money in the pockets of the people to buy back their full production. Therefore, there should be some supplementation of that money. The figure of $25 was grasped at and it stuck and, of course, forever afterward we were accused of promising $25 a month. The howl went up the other day that this was a far cry from that $25 a month, and the payment of the present dividend was ridiculed.
Now let me put the record straight, here. This dividend which is being given by the Alberta government to the citizens of the province of Alberta is not, in actual fact, a Social Credit dividend as proposed by Social Crediters. The recent announcement of the payment of an annual dividend to all citizens of Alberta from one-third of the oil royalties must not be regarded as a Social Credit dividend in the true sense but must be regarded as a return to Alberta citizens of a share of the income from the natural resources of that province-resources which really belong to them. The need for an actual Social Credit dividend as proposed by Social Crediters arises from the fact that there is never enough money coming out of the process of the nation's production to buy back the nation's total production at given prices. This results in a shortage of purchasing power, and to bring about a balance it is necessary at intervals to make a direct issue of additional new money and put it in the hands of consumers. This additional amount of money, created for this purpose and distributed among the citizens of Canada. is known as a Social Credit dividend.
Provincial governments do not have the constitutional power to create new money. The proposed Alberta dividend is simply a return to the people of money already issued and circulating through the regular channels of industry. As Premier Manning stated at a public meeting on the evening of March 1, the government is taking one-third of the revenues from the oil royalties and returning them in cash to the individual citizens of Alberta in their capacity as shareholders in "Alberta Unlimited".

The Budget-Mr. Legare
British Columbia announced last year that they would pay to the home owners of that province an amount of about $28 for the purpose of easing the tax burden, and action is now being taken with regard to this. This money is paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of that province. With dividends out west, and increasing taxation in the east, many thousands of people are becoming aware of the advantages of Social Credit administrations.
We have heard a lot in this debate in respect of inflation and, as the leader of this party said on one occasion, the generally accepted definition of inflation is too many dollars chasing too few goods. Now if that is a correct interpretation of inflation, I fail to see that we have inflation in Canada today, because of the fact that there are no goods in short supply. If there are any goods in short supply, I would like the minister, or any responsible minister of the government, to tell us exactly what goods are in short supply. Are we short of radios? Are we short of television sets? Are we short of musical instruments? Are we short of furniture? Are we short of clothes? Are we short of men's suits, or women's dresses? Are we short of boots and shoes? What are we short of? I have not been able to find out what we are short of.
I call upon the Ottawa Journal here,-a very good paper, sometimes,-and I note the advertising which it contains. Here is a whole page which Simpsons-Sears, trying to beautify our women, have taken to advertise women's dresses and things. Another page is advertising towels, another one, stockings; another one, draperies; another one, fur coats; another one,-oh, oh, I will not mention that,-and another one furniture, dining room suites-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to offer on the budget now before the house and on certain matters relating to it.
Since the budget was introduced, about ten days ago, I have had occasion to meet many of my constituents and to discuss with them the contents of the budget speech. I have found that by far the great majority of them were only too glad to accept it as

it is, because of the peculiar conditions now prevailing. I have also had occasion, like the rest of my colleagues, to read the newspaper comments on the budget speech. I have noted that some of the papers expressed the view that this budget was that of a brave man while others called it a family budget. Still, in the view of the opposition, this budget is supposed to be insignificant.
I wondered why the opposition chose that particular epithet, but soon realized that this budget was insignificant for them, since this year, as in other years, they were left with little else to do but to voice sterile criticism, thus remaining faithful to their own traditions.
To my mind, this is a realistic budget presented by a government which has only one concern in mind: the proper discharge of its mandate. It does so while continuing to work for peace and while ensuring a fair distribution of the revenues at its disposal and drawing ever closer the bonds which must unite, in justice and charity, Canadians of all tongues, races and creeds.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) deserves our appreciation and our compliments for the understanding which he has never ceased to show, and for the intelligence which he brings to bear on the problems of the hour as well as for the well considered solutions which he proposes.
No one can claim that this is an electoral budget. It hardly errs on the side of excessive generosity. It cannot be called extravagant. It was based on prevailing conditions, and again, its value is found in the suggested distribution of profits.
In the field of social security, it is less generous than we would have liked it to be. However, we may hope that, during the next sessions-as the government is going to stay in power-an ever-increasing amount will be earmarked for pensions and allowances. But, even if it were done, I do not believe the provincial governments should consider themselves freed from every responsibility in this respect.
The tax exemptions which shall now benefit contributors to a registered savings fund in view of retirement are a direct encouragement to thrift. Such action, on the part of the government, is a welcome step which should be followed by many others.
Too many people no longer have the sense of thrift and thoughtlessly spend income which could some day prove very helpful.
Mr. Speaker, though I was given the opportunity to be present at the eleventh

session of the United Nations which ended recently in New York, I do not propose to comment on the external policy of the Canadian government. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) have on many occasions stated our position. On the other hand, all members in this house have had occasion to observe the devices of the official opposition, specially in these last few weeks, with regard to the explosive situation in the Middle East. However, if members of our armed forces of the last wars covered themselves with glory on all battlefields and did honour to their country, an honour which they continue to enjoy, I have no hesitation in stating that our Secretary of State for External Affairs also covered himself with glory in all fields of diplomacy and that he has been a great credit to all Canadians.
I can understand that the opposition is jealous of his success and fame but I do not understand quite so readily why the same opposition is continuing to jeopardize the good relations of Canada with so many countries.
I cannot help but emphasize again the prestige enjoyed by our country at the United Nations. According to information I gathered from several delegates and from my own observation on the spot, I have not the shadow of a doubt that Canada is held in high esteem by nearly all countries of the world and that she has gained a prestige which even the greatest powers envy.
But this reputation our country is enjoying the world over, is not a mere accident. On the contrary, it is the result of the wise and cautious policy which has been followed for a good number of years. Its leader today is the worthy successor of the distinguished ambassador the leader of the government used to be and continues to be.
The hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs has played an unequalled part at the last session of the United Nations. I want to pay him my tribute as well as I want to emphasize the great work accomplished by his colleague the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), and I must also mention the great extent to which we are honoured in New York by the permanent representative of Canada to the United Nations, our ambassador, Mr. McKay. I have much pleasure therefore in pointing out the good relations he is maintaining with all the member countries of the United Nations. I have also been able to notice that he enjoys the finest of reputations among the representatives of the various countries.
The Budget-Mr. Legate
I will even go as far as to say, with respect to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that by proposing and obtaining the creation of a police force, he prevented the aggression of last October from degenerating into a world conflict. If you just consider the thousands of people killed by the intervention of the Russian army in Hungary, you can easily realize how many lives have been spared through the cease fire in Egypt.
The sub-committee on disarmament is now meeting in Great Britain and our country, apart from the big five powers, is the only one to sit there as a member. The sub-committee is a division of the Security Council of the United Nations and, as such, is considering any suggestion which could lead the universe to real peace.
To my mind it would be an important further step towards peace if it were possible to obtain from every member state of the United Nations that they file with the general secretariat of that organization their sales, purchases, exchanges and even gifts of conventional weapons and others. Canada has already offered a useful suggestion with regard to the giving of previous notice of atomic or nuclear tests. It would be a useful contribution to disarmament to bring about an end to the sale or secret gifts of weapons, this being a policy which threatens the balance of power of the smaller nations.
Mr. Speaker, during the last few weeks I had occasion to be present at the meetings of the committee on agriculture and colonization. It has been making particular study of Bill No. 157 which relates to assistance to be extended to the western farmers by the government. Incidentally, in the course of our discussions, we have once more touched upon the matter of crop insurance. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who was present at the meetings of the committee has repeated that crop insurance was a matter for the provinces and that the federal government had no business in that field.
Even if the matter is under provincial jurisdiction, I think we have now come to the point when the federal government should enter into negotiations with the provinces in view of some agreement which would protect our eastern farmers, whose crops also sometimes suffer from adverse climatic conditions.
Since I have been in this house I witnessed some rather sad experiences. Indeed, I remember that in the spring of 1955, farmers in eastern Quebec asked for federal assistance because, during the previous season, their crops had been almost totally destroyed by

The Budget-Mr. Legare the drought. I approached the Minister of Agriculture, and the right hon. member told me that the matter came under provincial jurisdiction, but that the federal government would be happy to intervene if the provincial government asked for such action.
And, since the province had made no request to them, the federal government could not help those who had thus suffered.
During the spring of 1956 new requests for assistance were made because, this time, the heavy rainfall of the preceding year had destroyed practically all crops in several counties of the lower St. Lawrence region; as a matter of fact, a survey made by the U.C.C. revealed that damages had reached the astronomical figure of $5 million in two or three counties of my region. I tried once more to get assistance from the federal government, but the answer I got was that nothing could be done unless the request came directly from the provincial government. However, as we all know, last year was an election year in the province of Quebec, and the provincial government agreed to give seed to the farmers affected by the loss of their crop the preceding year, but they got no assistance whatsoever to make good the double loss they had suffered the previous year.
I believe we have reached the point where we cannot let so great a section of the agricultural class depend on the whims of the weather. If, for instance, an area is afflicted by crop failure, the whole economy of the area is affected. First of all, the farmers themselves sometimes have to meet loan payments or have to make payments for agricultural machinery. They are then completely paralysed and can no longer meet their obligations. That is why I strongly urge the government to consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces with a view to establishing some sort of crop insurance or to amending Bill No. 157 so that it would apply not only to the western provinces but all provinces of the country.
On the other hand, the government could introduce a new bill to assist eastern provinces just as western provinces are assisted when the weather damages or destroys then-grain crop.
Before concluding my few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should also like to point out to the government the importance of considering further the possibility of promoting winter navigation between both shores of the St. Lawrence river. The population of the north shore increases at an incredible rate.
[Mr. Legare.l

It is even predicted that within ten years the population of the Saguenay area could double. Now then, that population which is already fairly large and which is expected to double suffers from a shortage of agricultural products. Its land is not suitable for cultivation whereas, on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, there are beautiful farms where crops are abundant and for which a market must be found. The north shore market would be the most appropriate one.
Unfortunately during the winter months the only means of communication between the north and south shore of the St. Lawrence is by plane. This means that the economy of these two areas is to all intents and purposes paralysed during that season. The time is not far off when shipping companies will be able to establish a continuous yearlong service between the two shores but this service will not be efficient unless the government provides icebreakers. I know that the Department of Transport already has icebreakers on the slips and that it will be in a position to answer the representations which will be made by the shipping companies maintaining this year-round service. Moreover, port facilities will have to be ensured to those companies. I once more express my confidence that the government will bring to this subject the attention it requires. I am convinced that the government will give most active consideration to the requests which I have already had occasion to bring to its attention and which have also been voiced by my colleague from Saguenay, who is here and who is most happy to join with me in this. If our requests were implemented by the government, they would most certainly make it possible for a year-long service to be maintained to both shores of the St. Lawrence, between my constituency and the constituency of Saguenay.
Mr. Speaker, since I am on the subject of shipping, I would also like to say that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) should continue to study the advisability of improving the port facilities at Trois Pistoles and Ste. Flavie, at either end of my constituency.
Now, Mr. Speaker, since it seems that we are nearing the end of the last session of this parliament, and since I will probably have no further opportunity to speak in this house before the opening of the next parliament, I would very much like to thank the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the ministers and their parliamentary assistants for the assistance which they have extended to me in the carrying out of my

mandate. On behalf of my constituents, I express the hope that all will be back here since the country still needs them.
