subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thought which comes to mind in discussing the budget for this year is that there was really no major concession made to the taxpayer. What concessions there were were so small and so unimportant as to make one wonder whether or not they were seriously made. Personally, I feel that the budget was an unrealistic document. In fact, there seemed to be no pattern to the minister's tax exemptions. It seemed to be rather a hit-or-miss sort of procedure which resulted in tax exemptions on a wide variety of articles, the importance of which can best be judged I think by the fact that out of sales and excise taxes presently collected of about $1,330 million, the tax saving to the consumer in this field will be something in the nature of $20 million.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that $20 million is a sizeable amount of money in itself. But I am sure that all would agree it is a mere drop in the bucket compared to $1,330 million which is presently collected in the form of sales and excise taxes. There is no doubt that the effects of high prices have taken their toll of the living standards of those who exist on fixed incomes. Meanwhile, the government goes placidly on its way spending more and more money, extracting more and more taxes from the taxpayers which, in latter years, has meant larger and larger surpluses despite the very considerable and very effective efforts of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to bury them here and there.
Probably the most disappointing aspect of the budget was the failure to recognize the plight of old age pensioners, and other pensioners, who have watched rising prices in the last few years completely outdistance their purchasing power. I was convinced that the government would introduce some sort of increased pensions to those people, but it never entered my mind that they would be so unrealistic as to confine the old age pension increase to the sum of $6 a month.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that as the members of this house go back to their constituencies they will find a growing uneasiness; they will find also an ill-concealed resentment against this small increase. Frequently in
The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough this house when we are called upon to accept what we consider to be less than had been expected in any field, the phrase is heard, "Well, while we do not approve we must consider that half a loaf is better than no bread". I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is not even half a loaf; in fact I think we would be stretching the point if we said it was even a slice of bread.
I was rather disappointed also that the minister, together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, did not consider some other amendments in the field of old age pensions. Possibly, Mr. Speaker, the matter about which I am going to speak more properly belongs to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but since I am speaking of old age pensions at the moment I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to representations that have come from several quarters for a reduction in the residence requirements for the recipients of old age pensions and those in receipt of old age assistance. It was in October or November of last year, at the federal-provincial welfare conference, that the minister of public welfare for the province of Ontario asked the federal government to reduce the residence requirements for recipients of old age pensions and old age assistance from 20 years to 10 years. It was pointed out at that time that two other acts which are sponsored by the federal government, namely the Disabled Persons Act and the Blind Persons Act, both require residence qualifications of 10 years. I draw this to the minister's attention once more, and I hope he will see fit to make this amendment to the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act.
I was somewhat surprised, Mr. Speaker, at the provision in the budget for a $100 exemption from taxable income of all taxpayers in lieu of charitable donations, medical expenses, and so on. I must say I heard this rumour about three or four years ago. I was told that the government was considering giving blanket coverage of a certain amount to all taxpayers. A couple of years ago in this house-it may have been last year, I am not too sure of the year-I asked the minister if it was true that taxpayers were permitted to deduct from taxable income $25 in lieu of charitable donations. At that time he said no. Yet, I knew that taxpayers were doing just that and that it was being accepted in three centres. I knew that.
Subsequent to the reply to me in the house I had several people come to me and say, "That is wrong; we do deduct $25 in lieu of charitable donations". Well, my reaction was

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough that if that was so, and was generally accepted in three centres, certainly there were a great many taxpayers across Canada who had been gypped out of their rights in this regard. However, apparently it was not a part of the law. I could not find it anywhere and the minister had said no, it was not true. Now in like manner a $100 donation coverage has been announced and will be brought in by the minister in the form of a resolution, I expect.
This brings up a point which might very well be considered by this house, Mr. Speaker. Although tithing is now a rather outmoded form of gauging one's charitable contributions, nevertheless there are many people who, to the best of their ability, give from their earnings to charitable causes, to their churches and to other religious organizations. In my own office I have clients who, strangely enough-I suppose some people would consider it strange-give so much to charity that they are unable to deduct all of their contributions. That is, they actually give to charity more than 10 per cent of their income. When we come to the point where we are making up their income tax returns we find we have to disregard some of the contributions they make to charity. On the other hand there are a great many people with quite substantial incomes who never contribute a nickel. Yet these persons who have heretofore given nothing are now going to be allowed to deduct $100 from taxable income because the department says it is more trouble to look for the receipts for the first $100, and it costs too much to examine them.
It has long been the belief of charitable organizations that one of the incentives to charitable giving, quite apart from the good will of the giver, was the fact that this amount was deductible from income for tax purposes. Now it is not necessary for a person who would be inclined to give a small amount to charity to give anything. He can claim $100 anyway, whether he gives anything or not. I think it is a backward step. Even if it costs the department more to examine those receipts than it would gain in taxes, I still believe the receipts should be produced; people should be forced to prove that they have actually expended this amount of money. The same is true of medical expenses, about which I wish to speak in a few moments.
It seems to me that instead of giving $100 additional exemption for charitable donations which do not exist, the government might have raised the statutory exemptions from $1,000 and $2,000 to $1,500 and $3,000. That would give relief where relief is needed. While it would have been a larger exemption, it would not have been that much larger. The slack would have been taken up to some

extent by the $100 exemption which is now given to those persons who in the past have given little or nothing to charity, because those are the people who are going to benefit. The taxpayer who previously gave $200, $300, $400, $500, $600 and more to charity still has to produce all his receipts. He does not get $100 in addition to the receipts he produces. He must still produce all of his receipts to claim the first $100. The chap who gives nothing, or less than $100, does not have to produce any receipts; he just claims the $100.
While I agree with the provision allowing $200 additional earning allowance for students-and I am sure this will be welcomed by many taxpayers who are finding it difficult to educate their sons and daughters, particularly in higher institutions of learning, where it becomes more and more expensive -yet I think the ceiling on permissible earnings could have been raised for the blind pensioners, for the war veterans and for old age pensioners under the Old Age Assistance Act.
However, although the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare made some slight adjustments in the ceilings, they were made only to about the extent of the increase in the old age pensions and other pensions. It seems to me that if $200 additional earning allowance could be given to students it could also have been given to those in receipt of old age assistance, war veterans allowance and blindness pensions.
I said a moment ago that I intended to say something about deductions for medicines. In this case again the person who spends a small amount will have his expenditure covered without any question being asked and yet the repeated requests on the floor of this house for the abolition of the 3 per cent floor for medical expenses have gone unheeded.
I had a few instances brought to my attention recently. In one case the taxpayer is obliged to pay $15 per month for medicine which is not included in those medicines now recognized by the department the expenditure for which is deductible from income. An expenditure amounting to $15 a month or $180 a year is a sizeable sum and yet the taxpayer cannot deduct any portion of that and the price of this particular product is steadily rising. This drug is keeping the taxpayer in question alive and yet he can deduct no part of the $15 a month expenditure.
In another case of which I have knowledge the taxpayer is a woman. I hold in my hand photostatic copies of invoices from the pharmacy from which she purchases the

drugs she needs. I also have a letter from the doctor who attends this patient and he indicates that for the rest of her life she will be required to take these two drugs, anso-lysen and trawill. These drugs cost her $31.25 per month but the amount so expended is not deductible from income for the purposes of income tax.
In both instances these people are of moderate circumstances and live in a part of town where ordinary working people dwell. You would not call it an area where those in higher income brackets live. Both are required to meet this expense in order to maintain themselves in good health and they receive no compensation whatever by way of income tax exemptions.
I do not wish to be unfair, Mr. Speaker, and I must point out that there are a couple of things in the budget with which I am pleased. For instance, I was pleased to see that the government is now prepared to permit self-employed persons to deduct from their taxable income the premiums which are paid for retirement pensions and annuities. I realize that this is a problem which requires a great deal of study but these deductions are permitted in other countries and now at long last our own government has seen fit to permit them. I am sure this will result in savings by self-employed persons which they otherwise would not be able to make and if there is anything at all in the budget, which is anti-inflationary in nature, Mr. Speaker, this is it.
I was also glad to see one other small item which I think is long overdue and I believe it has passed unnoticed in the discussion which has taken place on the budget so far. I am referring, of course, to professional fees paid by professional people which are now to be allowed as an exemption from salary.
In the rapidly changing world in which we live more and more people of professional status are employed on a salary basis by hospitals, in industry and in commerce. Such people including doctors, lawyers, accountants, engineers, and others find that in order to maintain their status it is necessary to pay fees to the professional group to which they belong in much the same manner as members of unions pay dues to their unions. Heretofore it has not been possible for professional people to claim exemption for the fees so paid. Representations have been made on their behalf repeatedly and I am pleased to see that the government now proposes to bring in an amendment which will permit this deduction.
Last year I referred to the interpretation that has been placed on clause 11 (1) (j) 82715-174
The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough with respect to the payment of alimony and the claim therefor from taxable income and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to it again. Speaking on this subject last July, I referred to the appeal which had been heard by Mr. Fordham, and to that part of his judgment where he said:
The matter reveals for the first time, where the board is concerned, what appears to be a remarkable and unfortunate oversight or omission in the drafting of the foregoing enactment.
Mr. Fordham pointed out that whereas alimony as such is quite clearly deductible when it follows a decree of divorce in cases like the one I referred to last year where there is merely a separation-even though the separation agreement had been executed by the husband and wife-the husband seeking to claim the alimony which he had paid iri pursuance of the terms of the separation agreement found it was disallowed.
Mr. Fordham made a very simple suggestion which would have rectified the situation had the minister seen fit to amend the act in the way it was suggested by him. I wish to raise this matter again this year because not only is it a question of the amounts paid in the way of alimony pursuant to separation agreements, but it is also a question of amounts that are paid into the family courts by persons who have not gone through a form of legal separation but where a husband continues to maintain his wife and child, usually under an order of the court. It seems to me that where these amounts are paid and can be proved to have been paid they should be deductible by the taxpayer.
There are many other cases that have come up in the course of the year, Mr. Speaker, where there appears to be considerable doubt as to the justice of the act with regard to specific taxpayers. Of course it is always the case that any law is likely to work a hardship on someone because it is almost impossible to draft an act which will give impartial treatment to all persons; but it seems to me that is why we have a board of appeal and persons in authority who are charged with the responsibility of making decisions in difficult cases. When those persons in authority find their sympathies are with the taxpayer but the very wording of the act itself prohibits their giving a decision in favour of the taxpayer, and when the board points out this fact and makes suggestions, it seems to me those suggestions should receive favourable consideration by the minister.
I have an account in my hand which was quoted in the Canadian Tax Journal dealing with a case where a woman lived apart

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough from her husband in a self-contained domestic establishment. She maintained therein herself, two children and her mother. During this one year she earned $3,200 in wages and received from her husband in accordance with an order of the family court-we have the family court coming into it again- $1,140 for the maintenance of herself and her two children.
She claimed the marital exemption of $2,000 as a person who had a child wholly dependent upon her. She claimed also the dependent's exemption of $150 for the second child and $400 in respect of her mother who was also wholly dependent upon her. The minister contended that her status was that of a single woman with one dependent, her mother, and that the payments made by the husband were not alimony since the parties were not legally separated and that the children were not wholly dependent upon her by reason of the payments made by the husband. When this case was reported in the tax journal it was headed with two words "Rough Deal?" It seems to me that people in these circumstances have enough to contend with without being penalized by the tax collector.
Some two or three weeks ago I placed on the order paper some questions with regard to revised assessments for 1950 and 1951. These questions were answered subsequently by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and disclosed that a number of re-assessments had been made in the dying days of 1956 before the amendment to the act brought in last year by the Minister of National Revenue became effective. Subsequent to those answers being received I also received a considerable amount of correspondence from various places in Canada as well as other information with respect to assessments which had been made at the end of 1956.
Some of these are extremely interesting because it seems to me that if an original assessment is made the department should be able to find out whether anything is wrong within a period of four years. When most people receive an assessment from the department and are told that they owe so much additional tax or are eligible for a refund, as occasionally happens, they consider that to be the final assessment. To all intents and purposes it is the final assessment unless within a reasonable length of time further information comes to light or unless, without regard to time, fraud is suspected.
The dates of some of these original assessments and subsequent re-assessments are extremely interesting. In one case the original assessment on the 1950 return was made

on May 30, 1951, the re-assessment being made on December 21, 1956. In another case the original assessment on the 1951 return was made on May 23, 1952, the re-assessment being made on December 21, 1956. I should like to point out that the instances which I propose to cite are all cases where had the re-assessment not been made by December 31 it could not have been made unless fraud had been indicated.
In another case the original assessment on a 1951 return was made on April 25, 1952 and it took the department until December 28, 1956, to make the re-assessment. I might point out that that was the last working day in 1956, the very last day before the revision of the act came into effect.
From another source I have a 1950 tax return which was assessed on May 23, 1951 and re-assessed on December 28, 1956, again the very last working day in 1956. I have another 1951 return which was assessed on May 16, 1952 and re-assessed on December 28, 1956. Another 1950 return was assessed on May 14, 1951; a 1951 return was assessed on May 27, 1952, and in both cases there was a re-assessment again on December 28, 1956.
So it goes on. I have in my hand an original assessment on a 1951 return which was made on May 23, 1952 and the taxpayer received a small rebate on May 28, 1952. His 1952 assessment was received on May 7, 1953 and it was indicated that there was no unpaid balance or refund. Both returns were reassessed on December 14, 1956.
It is a sad commentary to make to say that the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Finance do not see eye to eye on these matters despite the protestations of both ministers that they do. When this amendment to the act was brought down last year we expected that it would remove one of the difficulties in connection with tax payments and I refer to the trouble and expense caused to a taxpayer who receives a reassessment five or six years after his return has been filed. By that time he may have forgotten what was in the original return and it is difficult for him to disprove the reassessment. When the new act came into effect on January 1 of this year the Department of National Revenue tried to keep that door from closing by reassessing. It is then up to the taxpayer to prove that he does not owe the amount charged.
I would also direct the attention of the house to the fact that interest on these assessments is added yearly and in some of the cases I have the interest added to the assessment was more than one-third the amount of the assessment. Quite apart from

the justice or otherwise of last minute assessments of this character, it seems to me that the interest should date only from the date of the reassessment and not from the date of the original assessment. It means that the business life of a taxpayer is disrupted while he proceeds to prove that he does not owe these amounts. He must stand the cost of an appeal, and even if he does win he still owes these sums of money. It seems to me that the time lapse, which has now been corrected, should have been allowed to stand until the new year, rather than the old practice which meant the department had to scurry to get them in in the last month.
I would like to draw attention to another matter which was discussed at the conference of the Canadian tax foundation at Montreal last autumn. It bears on the interpretation which is placed on the word "misrepresentation" as it appears in section 46 of the act. I think I can do no better than quote one of the gentlemen who was on the panel. After attention had been drawn to the fact that the word "misrepresentation" was capable of several interpretations this gentleman, Mr. Macdonald, pointed out that the courts had already interpreted misrepresentation to include innocent misrepresentation, innocent omission and even innocent miscalculation.
It was suggested at that time that some certainty could be put into the section either by qualifying the word "misrepresentation" and making it read "fraudulent misrepresentation" or by removing the word "misrepresentation" entirely so it could be left to the courts to determine whether or not the taxpayer had committed fraud. It seems to me that with such wide latitude, even with the present four-year limitation on assessments, this particular section of the act should be cleaned up in order to make it more understandable to those who are charged with the responsibility of collecting taxes.
There is one other matter, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to mention with regard to taxes, and that is the field of succession duties. A revision of this act is, of course, overdue, and this was recognized a year ago by the minister when he indicated-probably I should not say "promised"-that he expected to bring down an amendment to the act, or otherwise revise the act, this year. It was in 1954 that the Minister of Finance referred in his budget address to a contemplated revision of the Dominion Succession Duty Act and now, three years later, we are still waiting for that revision. True enough he made one slight concession-it might almost be called a nod in the direction of the taxpayers-but he has paid no heed to the repeated demands 82715-174J
The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough which have been made for a straight exemption basis rather than the present basis which, amounts practically to confiscation of sums ini excess of the ceiling set.
In considering this matter we might gO' back to 1941, when the Dominion Succession Duty Act was first passed. The exemption allowed then to a widow was $20,000. Since that time, Mr. Speaker, the cost of living has increased by approximately 80 per cent and, as pointed out in the Canada Trust bulletin,, if $20,000 was considered to be a fair exemption for a widow in 1941 then $35,000 at least should be a fair exemption at the present time. It has long been contended that the contribution made by a man's wife to his estate is equal to his own and, accordingly, she should be allowed to claim half the estate free of duty. This contention is given effect where the deceased was resident in the province of Quebec, in some jurisdictions outside Canada, and in certain other cases.
Although some general measure of relief was provided in 1948, when the act was revised, and although the ceiling now is $50,000, we must still consider that since that time there has been an increase in the cost of living of more than 31 per cent; and if that is so, if that was a reasonable amount in 1948 then estates not exceeding $65,000 should be exempted from duty now. Whatever the amount, Mr. Speaker, it is my contention that the amount so designated should be a straight exemption for the purpose of succession duty.
I see that my time is rapidly running out, Mr. Speaker, so I would just like to ask the Minister of Finance in collaboration with the Minister of National Revenue to give heed to some of the matters I have mentioned today. Also I would like to reiterate the request I made to the Minister of National Health and Welfare with reference to the residence requirement for old age pensions.
In the beginning of my speech I called this an unrealistic budget, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is. When you take taxes off motorcycles but leave them on automobiles, which have become a necessity for most working people in this country; when you find the government spending its millions recklessly and at the same time urging every individual to cut down his spending, you begin to wonder in just what kind of a haze the government mind works; whether, indeed, the government has not taken leave of its budgetary senses.
Canada is a great and vital nation, and is growing rapidly. According to the preliminary report of the Gordon commission we should have by 1980 a population of nearly 27 million people in Canada. Certainly the next 20 or 25 years will see remarkable changes

The Budget-Mr. Lusby in all phases of our economy. But the big question today is, will it be a Canadian economy? If we continue to levy such excessive taxation as we are levying today, and the adverse trade balance continues as it is continuing at the present time, then I fear it will not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have this opportunity to express to the Minister of Finance my sincere congratulations upon the outstanding and statesmanlike budget which he presented in this house on the evening of March 14.
One needs no special insight or knowledge, of course, to assume that the work of formulating the contents of this budget was not that of the minister alone; that the final result represents a vast pooling of energy, experience and thought, participated in, indirectly at least, not only by the various members of the cabinet but by many other brilliant Canadian intellects. None the less, I think it is proper to regard the Minister of Finance as the chief and responsible architect of the completed structure. Therefore to him is the praise. This involves, naturally, the corollary that the criticisms of the opposition are directed primarily against him. But the irresolute weakness of those criticisms, as we have so far heard them, is itself a species of praise.
Of the three budgets the minister has now brought down it can be truly said-and I prophesy that it will prove equally true of his fourth, in 1958-that each has been designed for the greatest good of the greatest number, without departure, however, from sound economic and financial principles applicable to existing conditions.
The present budget admirably meets that test. Obviously, of course, as opposition critics are clearly aware, a wide downward revision of taxes would have curried a considerable meed of popularity. And I wonder whether those critics, given the opportunity to use and misuse the powers of a minister of finance, could have resisted the temptation to trip gaily along that pleasant path, ignoring the danger that its inevitable terminus under existing conditions would be ruinous inflation.
The minister in this respect has chosen to adopt the right, if not the easiest, course. On the one hand he has extended benefits where they can safely be extended; on the other he has adhered to those measures necessary to keep in curb the surging forces of inflation. I predict that the good common sense of the Canadian people will ensure their approval, and that during the next 12 months a continuing onward march of our economy at a sound and proper pace, and an equally

sound increase in our national prosperity and well-being, will provide full and ample justification of the combination of forethought, experience, prudence, and generosity which has gone to the making of this latest budget.
Speaking first from a national point of view, without regional implications, I wish to express my wholehearted approval of the steps taken to better the scale of various social benefits, which of course apply to Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The monthly increases in old age security and assistance payments and in pensions for the blind and disabled bring a very welcome measure of additional help to those receiving them.
I do not wish to imply that what has been done in this respect in any sense renders the field static. Far from it. But the action which has been taken now, within the ambit of sound financial and economic considerations, constitutes in my opinion a real assurance to present and future recipients of social security benefits that in this field, where the Liberal party has been the great and almost the sole Canadian pioneer and creator, that party will continue in the forefront of progress toward its ultimate goal, the complete shielding of every deserving citizen of the country from the evils of actual want and destitution.
Let us not forget that the attainment of such a goal involves far more than the mere wish and will to attain it. It requires also the development and strengthening of the economic and financial sinews of the nation to the point at which they can safely bear the attendant and necessarily tremendous fiscal burden thereby imposed upon them. The continuing growth and economic expansion of this country under the wise policies of the present government, combined with the record and declared aims of the Liberal party, are the firmest guarantee our people can have of steady advance and improvement in the whole field of social security until the ultimate goal I have mentioned is fully reached.
In assessing recent advances in the social security field, one must add to the current increases in payments the advantages of the hospital and diagnostic services plan devised by this government and now, we hope, near the point at which it can be prepared for operation. Another new measure initiated by this government during the life of the present parliament and now scheduled for increased payments is the disability pension. Let me say in this connection that I hope that in the near future, with the necessary provincial co-operation, it will be

possible to relax the stringency of the provisions covering the degree of disability required to qualify for this pension. As I said before, the field of social security is not static, nor will it become so in future years while this government remains in power. The achievements I have mentioned are, I believe, the surest earnest of continuing Liberal progress in that field.
Of the various upward revisions of pensions and other payments provided for by the budget, none, I think, will meet with stronger approval by the Canadian public than the increases in the rates of the war veterans disability pensions, including widows' pensions and married war veterans allowances. In ancient times the old or disabled soldier was all too often left to shift for himself. It seems to me that the situation that prevailed in earlier days perhaps can best be expressed in Kipling's lines:
All the world over, nursing their scars,
Sit the old fighting men, broke in the wars . . . Dust of the battle o'erwhelmed them and hid. Fame never found them for aught that they did; Wounded and spent to the lazar they drew, Lining the roads where the legions roll through.
To the shame of mankind war has lost nothing of its horrors. Science, which should be devoted exclusively to human welfare and advancement, has only too largely been perverted to the devising of novel and more dreadful methods of destruction. Nevertheless many nations have experienced a great awakening of the conscience as to their duty to care and provide for those who have fought their battles. No longer is the old soldier left to languish by the roadside.
Canada prides itself upon the manner in which it has accepted and is discharging its duty in this field. Its record in that respect is unsurpassed by any other country in the world, and this latest provision of more generous assistance to the veterans and their dependents shows clearly that the determination remains that the record shall continue to be unsurpassed. With such an aim every loyal Canadian citizen is in full accord.
On this general topic I should like to make one suggestion. It is in regard to veterans of the first world war who served in the United Kingdom but not on the continent, and who are therefore not considered to have served in a theatre of actual warfare, as is required in order for non-pensioned world war I veterans to qualify for the allowance. It seems to me that any Canadian soldier who crossed the submarine-infested Atlantic in the days of 1914-18 ventured his life far in the defence of his country. Whatever the theory of hardship and shortening of life expectancy may be, I have always considered it somewhat anomalous that any such soldier
The Budget-Mr. Lusby should be deprived of the benefits of the War Veterans Allowance Act merely through the often purely fortuitous circumstance that he saw no service in France.
The budgetary matters upon which I have so far touched are of general application to Canadians in whatever section of the country they may live. Inevitably, however, members of the house representing constituencies in the Atlantic provinces must focus their attention upon those parts of the budget and of the minister's budget address which set out the far-reaching measures now to be undertaken for the purpose of stimulating the economy of those provinces.
In my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I described this budget as outstanding and statesmanlike. From the point of view of the Atlantic provinces I can go further and say it is a truly memorable budget. It represents, I submit, a new, active and eager acceptance by the government of the challenge presented by the differential in economic levels and general prosperity as between the Atlantic region and the other parts of Canada. During my term of membership in the house perhaps my most dwelt-upon topic has been the necessity of substantially reducing that differential if Canada is to become a really great, really united and really fortunate nation.
The solution is not an easy one, and it has grown increasingly evident that in view of the limited financial and economic resources of the provinces concerned, a substantial measure of federal co-operation and assistance is essential if the problem is to be effectively grappled with. The measures which the government is now ready to undertake are, in my opinion, both beneficial and substantial and in themselves will carry us an appreciable distance toward our ultimate goal.
The preliminary report of the Gordon commission, in so far as it dealt specifically with the Atlantic region, was greeted in my part of the country when it came out some two months ago with considerable misgiving, alarm and even denunciation. This was most evident with regard to its suggestion that under certain circumstances residents of the Atlantic provinces might be assisted to move elsewhere. Unfortunately the meaning and intent of the report were subjected to marked distortion and misinterpretation, often, I regret to say, by public figures who knew or should have known better.
I am glad the chairman of the commission has taken the opportunity, in an address in Halifax last month, to correct this state of affairs which, indeed, had already been largely corrected. He has shown what was evident to any serious student of the report

The Budget-Mr. Lusby in the first place, that the document contains a careful and realistic appraisal, a valuable appraisal, of the special economic problems confronting the Atlantic provinces. Certainly nothing is to be gained by an ostrich-like ignoring of the inescapable fact that such problems exist.
It has been made clear too that, far from being held up as a desirable policy, any assisted movement of people from the Atlantic region was mentioned only as a last resort if it proved impossible for them to earn there what they considered an adequate living. The real aim of the report, in outlining our problems and suggesting means of overcoming them, was to chart a road for the avoidance of any such last resorts. The chairman of the commission in his Halifax speech showed confidence that such a road can and will be followed into a bright future, a confidence I am happy to share with him and with the great majority of thoughtful people in the Atlantic region.
As Mr. Gordon also pointed out, the report indicated that much can be essayed at the federal level to eliminate or alleviate the difficulties which beset the Atlantic economy. It also outlines specific courses of action which may be taken by this government for that purpose. There were not wanting voices from the opposition benches in the house to prophesy that whatever the merits or demerits of the report, it would be promptly relegated to some dusty governmental pigeonhole and forgotten. Where are the mouths now that uttered that false prophecy? They are closed, Mr. Speaker, shut once and for all, on this particular point at least, by the budget. As we study the measures the government now proposes to undertake for the betterment of the Atlantic provinces, we can turn to any such opposition critics and invite them to view the first fruits of the Gordon report.
The Minister of Finance in his budgetary address outlined among other things two concrete measures of the utmost importance to the Atlantic region. One is the increase in freight subventions under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. The other, which awaits only agreement by the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, is the creation of a general grid system for electrical power covering those two provinces, with the federal government providing the main interconnecting facilities and building and operating such large thermal plants as are required to generate the electricity.
Neither government nor individual can alter the geography which separates the maritime provinces and Newfoundland from the markets of central Canada. But the 50 per

cent increase, from the previous 20 per cent to 30 per cent of the total cost, in the freight subventions on goods bound for those markets from the Atlantic region will go far to offset the untoward effects of geography. The benefits of this increase will accrue to every section of the region and nowhere, I believe, more than to my own constituency. Almost every phase of the much diversified economy of Cumberland county will experience a stimulus; the farming, the lumbering, the industries of Amherst, the coal mining of Springhill and elsewhere, and many of the numerous other economic pursuits my constituents follow.
It may be that the second concrete measure I have mentioned will have an even stronger appeal to the people of my county. Certainly it will to some. The exceedingly generous offer of this government to facilitate the creation of a general grid system for electrical power throughout Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, with such large central thermal generating plants as may be needed, represents the implementation of recommendations not only of the Gordon report but of the earlier Christie report as well, which we also owe to federal initiative.
The present proposal leads one to think first of cheaper power. Thermal generation of power on the large scale contemplated will certainly lower the cost substantially, and undoubtedly cheaper power is a prime need of the maritime provinces. I believe it is estimated that power may be as much as 30 per cent cheaper. Everyone there who uses electricity in any way, whether an urban householder or a farm operator, will share in the benefits. But the greatest boon will be to the industries of the area. Cheaper power, by placing maritime industries in a stronger competitive position, can do much to stimulate that industrial expansion which is a growing need of the region. Here again much advantage will accrue to the town of Amherst in my constituency, one of the leading industrial centres of Nova Scotia.
But this is only one side of the story. The world-wide decline in the use of coal as a source of heat and energy seems to have been, for the time being at least, arrested. In fact the trend even shows signs of reversing itself. In the long perspective coal is probably assured of a place of continuing, perhaps even increasing, importance. This emphasizes the national need to bolster the Canadian coal industry. None the less, I need hardly tell this house that the Nova Scotia coal industry faces serious marketing problems. The drawbacks of the lengthy haul to markets in central Canada, though eased by the freight and coal subventions, still remain. Increasing competition from other forms of fuel is inevitable.

The ceaseless need to lower costs of production will, to some extent at least, be met by the cheaper electrical power resulting from the contemplated interprovincial grid system. But apart from that, the use of coal in generating plants of the system will provide an expanded domestic market for Nova Scotia coal, a need foreseen by the Gordon report.
I wish to call particular attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that for the combined territorial unit of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and in fact for all three maritime provinces, the coal fields of my constituency are the most centrally located of any. A large central pithead power plant at Springhill, augmenting the plant already established in the Joggins-River Hebert area, seems to be a logical development in connection with the proposed interprovincial grid system. Incidentally I might add, as a sort of historical note, that the first pithead power station in Canada, and I rather think in North America, was established at Chignecto in my constituency early in this century. Every branch of the Nova Scotia coal industry will occupy a prominent place amongst the numerous beneficiaries of this promising power program. Add to those beneficiaries the many who will reap substantial advantage from the increased freight subsidies, and the two measures put forward by the federal government will together constitute as potent a stimulus to economic and particularly industrial activity in the maritimes as we have seen in many a day. For that reason I call this, Mr. Speaker, from the Atlantic point of view a memorable budget.
It is not suggested, of course, that it provides a complete answer to all the economic problems of my part of the country. It is thus gratifying to know that, as the Minister of Finance has said, the government is conducting further active studies on the possibilities of stimulating the development of the Atlantic region. A generally improved transportation system is, as the Gordon report states, an evident need of the region. In this connection I wish to mention one subject which was not touched upon by that report, the Chignecto canal.
Advocates of the canal are fond of using the argument, which is founded on fact, that the canal was promised at confederation. No doubt that argument is entitled to some weight. I have never concerned myself so much with the question of whether it was promised or needed in 1867 as with the question of the need for it now and in future years, and of the advantages it would confer upon the Atlantic region and, indeed, upon many other parts of Canada. It seems to me that a map is one of the strongest arguments
The Budget-Mr. Lusby in favour of the Chignecto canal, for it shows at a glance how in this instance unfavourable geography can be largely circumvented.
As an addition to the internal transportation system of the Atlantic provinces the canal, by providing a short, cheap water passage between many parts of the four provinces now linked only by long and circuitous sea routes, would in my opinion be of inestimable value. Then, again, the canal would afford to all those areas of our Atlantic region bordering on Northumberland strait and the gulf of St. Lawrence a direct and vastly shortened water route to the New England states. May I point out that only very recently a prominent spokesman of those states declared that there is developing in New England a need, a crying need he termed it, for many primary products of the Atlantic provinces. The possibilities here of enhancing trade by means of the canal are obvious.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, we now see Canada in the process of unprecedented growth and economic expansion. Bearing this in mind; bearing in mind the swiftly advancing development of the vast iron ore deposits in northern Quebec and Labrador, the mineral discoveries in northern New Brunswick and the coming completion of the St. Lawrence seaway it is, I submit, as inevitable as sunrise that there will be a hugely increased volume of seaborne traffic between the river and gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic coast of the United States. The Chignecto canal can shorten the route of such traffic by hundreds of miles. Remember, too, that in the event of war this canal would enable this great volume of strategic shipping to avoid the perils of a long voyage through the open Atlantic.
The U.S.S.R., as we know only too well, is concentrating on building modern submarines in vast numbers. If war comes their menace will dwarf that which even Hitler's U-boats offered. We may be certain that a large proportion of the Russian submarines would be detailed to haunt the waters of our Atlantic coast. The Chignecto canal would offer to shipping between the gulf of St. Lawrence and American ports, in place of the long, exposed route which is now the only one available, a far shorter and easily protected and defended one. In a brief period of war our saving in shipping losses would soon exceed the entire cost of the canal.
In view of what I have mentioned, I consider it of the utmost importance that the question of the Chignecto canal be thoroughly reviewed once more in the light of modern conditions. Such a review, involving careful examination of many economic, engineering, strategic, and other factors, should in my

The Budget-Mr. Lusby opinion be entrusted to a special royal commission. I hope that in its study of the transportation problems of the Atlantic provinces the government will bear this in mind.
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that both the increase in freight subsidies and the provision of cheaper electric power in the mari-times through the proposed grid system would prove a valuable stimulus to industry in the area.
In this connection, however, I hope that another recommendation of the Gordon report will not be overlooked. That is the recommendation that a greater number of defence production orders be placed in the Atlantic region.
The town of Amherst in my constituency is, as I said before, one of the leading industrial centres of the maritimes. Its diversified manufacturing plants are capable of undertaking a very considerable range of defence production orders. I have in mind particularly the two chief industries of the community, the aircraft division of Enamel and Heating Products Limited, and Robb Engineering Works Limited, a subsidiary of Dominion Bridge Company Limited. These industries are no strangers to defence production contracts which have, indeed, constituted a most important factor in the industrial activity of the town both during and since world war II. That they have the capacity, the experience, the knowledge and the reliable skilled working forces necessary to carry out any defence production contracts assigned to them is amply demonstrated by their past records, which will stand comparison with any in Canada.
A definite policy of assigning to the Atlantic region a more generous share of defence contracts would ensure the operation of these and many other industries at a steadier and reasonably high rate of activity. Further, it would be a definite factor in combating the over-concentration of industry in the central provinces. We have heard much in this house in the past of the evils of such overconcentration, and I submit that a wider spreading out of industry across Canada would bring nothing but benefit to the whole country. In peace it would mean a broader general diffusion of prosperity. In time of war a wide decentralization of vital industries would be of superlative importance in the interests of national safety and the defence effort.
Occasionally even authorities in the central provinces express themselves as concerned with the undue concentration of industry there, though they never seem to entertain such views quite forcefully enough to prevent their grabbing for every new


industry they can get. But the federal government, by means of such a policy as I mention, can do something to rectify the situation. Even if the carrying out of such a policy should involve a moderate increase in costs, I submit that this would be more than offset by the resulting benefits to the nation viewed as a whole.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to leave that suggestion with the government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I had occasion to disagree with the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

I want to take this opportunity to put it right. I might say that His Honour the Speaker told me that I could not do it when I wanted to do it and felt like doing it. I want to straighten it out now before I say anything else. The minister said, as reported at page 2609 of Hansard of March 22, 1957:
With regard to disability allowances, no one in this house who has criticized the government, including the last speaker who spoke so amusingly, has mentioned the increase provided for disability allowances, and I am not aware that anyone in this house in this session or in the last session has ever asked the government to increase the basic amount of disability allowances.
From questions I have asked the minister from time to time he must be aware of my keen interest in disabled and blind persons and the old age pensioners. If the minister would care to look up page 313 of Hansard for January 16 of this year, when I spoke in the speech from the throne debate, he will see where I went into the matter in detail. I will quote a few passages from that page to prove that I dealt with this question:
I wonder whether the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who was here a minute ago, has any information to give the house regarding the Disabled Persons Act. I have spoken to the minister at different times and asked him if he was sure that every province was administering the act in the same way. I said that some provinces were very strict in their administration of the act while others seemed more human, although the minister had previously explained that the regulations were drawn up in co-operation with the provinces.
Further on I said:
I do not wish to take the time of the house by dwelling further on the subject of old age pensions as most hon. members have already drawn the attention of the government to the need for an increase in the pension rate. I think that feeling is widespread in this house; people everywhere have been getting up and asking for increased old age pensions. When everybody is agreed, and the attention of the government has been drawn to this matter, then I think a reform is long overdue. The $40 which an aged citizen gets today has the value of only $20 compared with purchasing power in the past, and in the light of the continual rise in the cost of living which is taking place it is

essential that the government should give immediate consideration to providing a decent living for those people who have helped to build the Canada that we inherit today.
Then a few lines farther down the page I said-

Lastly I appealed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to give serious consideration to the plight of the disabled person, the blind person and the old age pensioner. I said:
It appears that in our efforts to build a better Canada we are inclined to forget the people who need help most.
I hope the minister is going to withdraw the statement he made that nobody was worrying about the old age pensioner or the disabled pensioner. I have tried in as short a time as I could to prove-and I am speaking for myself-that I am one of the members of the house who raised this matter not only this year but last year. I am going to say no more about it, Mr. Speaker. I think the minister will give me credit for having brought the matter up.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I see the minister smiling; he must be saying something pleasant.
I was indeed pleased to see that the Minister of Veterans Affairs saw fit to increase the veterans pensions. I personally think the Minister of Veterans Affairs stopped short when he did not carry this through to include single veterans and widows' allowances, as their present allowances are inadequate to provide them with decent living conditions. While the permissible income of the single veterans and widows has been raised, the unfortunate thing is that most of these people are getting too old to go out and earn more income. I hope the minister will give this matter some consideration.
I was pleased to see in the budget that an amendment will be made to allow claims for the care of retarded children to rank as medical expenses. I come from the town of Selkirk, where there has recently been set up a class for retarded children. One of the great problems they have is the transportation from their homes to the school each day. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance will make a note of it and let me know if this is regarded as medical expenses for the care of these retarded children.
I have some remarks to make on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, but I shall leave them until the amending bill is before the 82715-175
The Budget-Mr. Bryce house. Every day one finds on his desk a complaint of some kind dealing with farm problems.
During the last ten years the farm has undergone great changes; we have seen the horse disappear and everything become mechanized. Mechanization has cost a lot of money, and farm machinery is so expensive that it is no longer good business to have just a quarter section. One has to have more acres to work in order to make farming economically sound. When a young man buys a farm on which to get started it represents a big undertaking today. The mechanization has vastly built up the cost of producing cattle or grain compared to what it was when we were in the horse era.
A few days ago we had a discussion in the house concerning eggs and the floor price. According to the report of the poultry products marketing board of the Department of Agriculture of Canada, imports of dressed poultry in 1955 were 15,255,823 pounds, and in 1956 they were 22,816,809 pounds. Up to March 8 of this year 1,467,424 pounds had been imported. Looking at the importation of eggs as at the week ending December 29, 1956, the report shows that 68,321 cases were imported, and for the same period a year ago 20,921 cases were imported. This importation of poultry and eggs must have a depressing effect on our market, and the farmer is wondering how long this sort of thing will continue.
While I am dealing with the subject of poultry I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the grading of turkeys. I shall confine my remarks to turkeys and shall not deal with chickens, but the same thing could be applied to them. On other occasions I have suggested that when a turkey is graded it should maintain that grade until it reaches the consumer's table. If it is graded an A turkey it should have this grade stamped on it, perhaps by a disc or a clip of some kind on the corner of its wing, and the same thing would apply to the other grades. If this was done the farmer would be satisfied that he was getting the proper grade for his turkeys, and the consumer would also be satisfied that he was getting a square deal.
Farmers in the interlake area are of the opinion that it does not pay them to produce eggs if the price goes down to 30 cents per dozen. The floor price on eggs should be 38 cents at the producer's level instead of 30 cents per dozen for grade A large eggs f.o.b. Winnipeg. From what I read in briefs and farm magazines and from what I gather in talking to producers it is evident that the

The Budget-Mr. Bryce price of eggs is a sore point with poultry farmers in many parts of Canada, and something should be done about it.
The marketing of livestock also presents a serious problem, and with the rise in the farmer's costs he will have to find a system that will give him the highest possible return. The interprovincial farm union council in their presentation to the government of Canada on February 19, 1957, said this: Merchandising and marketing-
In designing a marketing system for farm products, certain requirements must be met. In our opinion, the more important of these are:
1.	Cost should be at a minimum so that the producer can obtain the greatest possible share of the consumer's dollar.
2.	Adequate supplies of high quality produce should at all times be available to the consumer.
3.	The price received by the producer should quickly reflect changes in production costs.
4.	The presence of temporary surpluses should not be allowed to depress domestic prices.
The farm unions believe that these requirements can best be met by provincial producer-controlled marketing boards, operating in the domestic market -and national boards operating in the export market. The primary responsibility of the national boards would be to remove and dispose of surplus production so that these surpluses would not interfere unduly with domestic marketing.
We appreciate the fact that the farm organizations must accept primary responsibility in this field but, because of the magnitude of the task and the legislative basis of any action, we would respectfully request assistance on the following matters:
1.	We request the fullest co-operation of the federal government with the provincial governments in paving the way for establishment of producer marketing boards. We realize that this government, by establishing producer marketing board legislation, has recognized the value of such a marketing system.
2.	We request expanded economic research in marketing problems so that marketing schemes can be established on the soundest possible economic basis.
3.	We request continued research on the storage of farm products. Any improvements in techniques would greatly facilitate the orderly marketing of these products.
4.	We request the fullest co-operation of this government and the provincial governments in whatever new or amended legislation may be necessary to place marketing schemes on a sound legal basis.
5.	We request a review of the grading situation. A fairly comprehensive system of grading has been established for most farm products, but we have reason to be concerned over the interpretation and application of these grades from time to time, and over the fact that the benefits from rigorous application of these standards at the farm level are not always passed on to the consumer.
I have another matter which I should like to discuss, concerning which I have been receiving many complaints. I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture or perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the importation of powdered milk and cheese, which is worrying the cream producer and the small creameries that are the backbone of the dairy industry. This problem is of concern not only to the

producers in the interlake country but to those in many districts in Manitoba. Perhaps I can best illustrate this problem by quoting from the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented to the cabinet on February 15, 1957, which I think will explain the situation fairly well. On page 11 of the brief the following statement appears:
With respect to skim milk powder and cheese dairy producers are convinced that not only are the special duties of one cent per pound on imports from Australia and New Zealand completely unrealistic, but also that the present regular British preferential tariff on these products is unreasonably low. This is especially evident in view of the very favourable natural conditions for dairy production which exist in New Zealand and Australia and especially in the former country.
In the case of skim milk powder the Canadian Federation of Agriculture requests that the Canadian government negotiate the elimination of the special tariff agreements with Australia and New Zealand and further that it negotiate a British preferential tariff on milk powder of 4 cents per pound, the same as the present most favoured nation rate.
In the case of cheese we request that the special Australia and New Zealand rates be similarly eliminated and the tariff raised to 6 cents per pound. In the absence of such a tariff increase cheddar cheese should be priced on the export-import control act list of products which may enter this country only under special permit.
We would further request that a floor price of 14 cents per pound on roller powder and 16 cents per pound on spray process powder be established, with at the same time a listing of this product under the export-import control act. An adequate level of returns for milk powder is necessary if the combined return to the producer for butter fat and skim milk is to reach levels which are at all adequate.
I hope that the recommendations and various points I have brought before the ministers will be given consideration. I have quoted from both the Canadian Federation of Agriculture brief and also that of the interprovincial farm union council. Both these organizations represent thousands of farmers in the Dominion of Canada. I am sure their reason for presenting these briefs is to improve their standard of living as farmers or dairymen, whatever the case may be. As I have already said, farming 10 or 15 years ago was quite different from the farming of today, and new rules and regulations will have to be made to meet these conditions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I add my congratulations to those tendered already to the Minister of Finance upon the most excellent budget which he has presented. We in this house who have known the minister for years feel that this budget is typical, because we know he is always conscious and careful of the money of other people, especially the money of the little people. On behalf of the little

people in my constituency I want to extend to him their congratulations and thanks.
The purpose of social legislation is not to take care of all the desires or needs of the constituents of Canada, it is to relieve them of the oppression of fear brought about by old age and other factors. This fear has been further relieved by the actions of the Minister of Finance and the government through this budget.
It is interesting to note that the number of old age security recipients in Ontario last year was about 283,171. These payments were not subject to any means test and were paid by the federal government. In addition there were those persons between the ages of 65 and 70 years who were in receipt of old age assistance, and these totalled 21,731. Then there is another class of persons who receive supplementary old age assistance. This supplementary old age assistance cannot exceed $10 per month, and must be initiated by the municipality.
I was most interested in reading what Hon. Dana Porter, the provincial treasurer, had to say on February 21, 1957, as reported on page 531 of the provincial Hansard. He said that more than 5,000 persons throughout Ontario are now benefiting from supplementary old age assistance payments, of which the province pays 60 per cent and the municipality the remainder. It is not correct to assume that Ontario is paying the supplementary payment of $10, because as this works out in Ontario the basic old age assistance would be $40 per month, of which $20 is contributed by the federal government and $20 by the provincial government. If it is necessary to grant a supplementary old age assistance payment of $10, $6 of that would be paid by the province and $4 by the municipality. I know that my own municipality is hard pressed to meet these payments of $4 per month to the recipients of supplementary old age assistance.
I do not suppose there is any other constituency in Canada which has more reason to be grateful for the social legislation which has been brought in by the Liberal government, in particular the Unemployment Insurance Act. This act has been of incalculable benefit to my constituency, especially during the past few months when the rate of unemployment has been exceedingly high. We are not crying about this, we are not complaining about our lot, we are going ahead to take steps to help ourselves. We are pursuing whatever action is possible along these lines.
As a matter of fact the mayor of Windsor, the heads of the unions and other civic representatives have been to Ottawa to discuss 82715-175J
27, 1957
The Budget-Mr. D. F. Brown this matter with government officials. Departments here in Ottawa have been busy assembling information which we trust will be of help to the municipality. As of yesterday, officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce have been in my city to see what could be ascertained to be of assistance to the community as a whole. Following along prearranged lines the mayor of the city has arranged a conference for next Tuesday, to which I received a telegram of invitation this morning. This conference will explore the possibilities of self-help, and will be attended by government representatives from Ottawa. I am not sure whether Ontario will be represented, but I assume it will. They will join with other civic representatives in an attack on this problem.
This debate affords me an opportunity to discuss another matter which is of national and international importance. We in Canada are spending many millions of dollars each year on national defence.
No one can deny the necessity for such expenditure under present conditions, yet it is not bringing us any nearer the goal of international peace. We in Canada, too, are contributing other millions to the total amount donated by a few countries of the western democracies to those countries which are poverty stricken and, of course, such generosity is commendable. But bestowing material gain on those countries has certainly not lessened international tension.
One of the greatest obstacles to world harmony is the problem of illiteracy. This must be overcome through the understanding of common justice and integrity. If the United Nations organization is to succeed it is essential that its efforts must be directed more and more to this most vital problem. The aim of the United Nations is, of course, to maintain international peace and security. It is not a world government but a forum for the discussion of problems of international importance. It is in large measure an apparatus whose function it is to focus world opinion on any current problem. I therefore submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if it can keep its member countries in discussion, eventually reason will prevail and bloodshed be averted. So long as they talk they will not fight.
But the United Nations must also, in the words of the preamble to its charter, "establish conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations arising from treaties and other sources of international law can be maintained". Hence the impact of the work of this great body is greatest on those countries where there is an informed and educated public opinion, countries

The Budget-Mr. D. F. Brown where the individual is free to think and to act. It is not sufficient that we have abundant book learning and broad technical skill. We must be free to demonstrate our knowledge and to criticize our superiors. We must be able to vote freely.
You will agree Mr. Speaker, that respect for the principle of the United Nations charter and the achievement of its purposes calls for the application of high ethical standards, standards as high and as noble as those which are an integral part of the great religious movements of the world. We all must face the challenge of making persistent and determined efforts to examine international problems with all the honesty we possess; soberly, in a spirit of good will, always endeavouring to understand the other fellow's point of view, free from malice and preconceived prejudices. Let us he honest, tolerant and restrained.
I said a moment ago that we must have an informed public opinion. What has been the situation? When the United Kingdom and France intervened in the trouble between Israel and Egypt we were shocked. Severe criticism arose not only in other countries but in France, and particularly in the United Kingdom. Some government members resigned in the United Kingdom, and resentment was very high. When the general assembly of the United Nations called upon these two countries to withdraw, both countries complied with the terms of the resolution. Public opinion demanded it.
But what did we find in the case of Hungary? There it was different. The Hungarian people arose against the communist tyranny but were brutally suppressed by the Soviet army. The United Nations stood by helplessly. The assembly passed four resolutions. One called for the withdrawal of Soviet forces. The second called for free elections. The third asked for the admission of U. N. observers, and the fourth called for contributions of food, medical supplies and aid to refugees.
The condemnation of Soviet action and the attempt to send in observers were brushed aside by the communists, confident in their belief that they had the strength to disregard public opinion abroad and to keep it in control in their own land. They were ready, however, to accept immediate shipments of medical supplies and food. It is astounding to see how many condemn the United Kingdom and France for what happened in Egypt, yet are quite indifferent to the tragedy of Hungary.
To be effective it would appear that the United Nations need an informed public opinion in the various countries of the world.

There is a serious need also for an educated public opinion. If the democratic countries find that in matters of vital national interest they must bow to the pressure of world opinion, and must follow a course of action which is ignored by countries less sensitive to such pressure, there is grave danger that the rule of law will be impeded. Thus the aim of maintaining international peace and security will be jeopardized. All countries must honour the principles, not merely the words, of the charter which they have accepted, and the same standard of conduct must be expected of all if we are to have the reign of international justice. There can be no double standard.
It is essential, I suggest, to have an informed and educated public opinion. But how can this be arrived at in countries which are governed by a feudal system wherein the rulers amass huge wealth and the common people have little? What can we do in countries where most of the natives are tenants of absentee landlords? What is the hope in a country where the life expectancy of the individual is less than 30 years, and where his annual income is about $41? We should seriously consider what our approach to the problem, which is of vital importance, should be if we are to establish conditions under which justice and the respect for treaty obligations in international affairs is to gain strength. Should we not appeal rather to the masses of people in underdeveloped countries rather than to governments?
One billion one hundred million people- that is about two-thirds of the population of the world-can neither read nor write. They are voiceless. They cannot vote. They are virtual slaves in one way or another. Almost all are in debt all their lives, yet they know not how much the debt is and they have no idea how to compute the interest.
Such conditions breed suspicion when there should be confidence in their leaders. They breed treachery without an understanding of events. They breed dishonesty without aiming to be so. They breed a trust in material things as all-important.
A few years ago I was on a mission in South America, 1,500 miles the other side of the equator, to Bolivia where over 90 per cent of the population are native Indians. In that country most of the land is owned by absentee landlords, persons living in faraway countries but certainly not at an altitude of 12,000 feet above sea level. There I observed that the peasants lived in houses built with adobe brick, which is sun-dried mud. The houses had thatched roofs made of material taken off the farms. Each house consisted of one room with one window at the end of the room, and the doorway was

covered with a homemade blanket. Plowing was done with the crotch of a tree. Cows were used to pull the tree crotches. The cows produced milk, but because of the condition of the cattle the milk could not be consumed except in the form of cheese.
There were 11 countries represented at the conference, most of them countries where similar conditions prevailed to one degree or another. I had many discussions about these matters with various high government officials and also the president of the country, but in order to get grass-roots information I was particularly interested in the views and opinions of the missionaries. I talked with Roman Catholic, Baptist, Methodist and Friends-they are the Quakers -missionaries.	I found they were doing
much to improve conditions, but there is certainly very much more to be done.
The missionaries had established a hospital which was in operation taking care of the sick, and they were maintaining clinics for education and giving training to student nurses. Generally they were setting a very good example to the residents, doing much to raise the standards of cleanliness, order and health and at the same time instilling in the mentality of the patients a strength of mind and character. Schools were set up to teach the youngsters, most of them operated by missionaries. Never was there need of an attendance officer for the students, because they were eager to learn to read and write in their native language. By practice and by precept they were given the letter and the spirit of a better way of life. The more enlightened students were encouraged to go on to higher courses which equipped them in turn to teach their brothers, and so there were many Indians trained to teach Indians. Instruction and assistance were provided in establishing better homes and gardens. The result was better crops and habitations.
Such plans as the Colombo plan do much to help the people of these eastern countries to help themselves. We give money and technical advice to build dams, to erect
The Budget-Mr. D. F. Brown power plants and to construct railroads. Yet the people are illiterate. They are still in slavery. The native has been told not only by the communists but by the democrats that he has the right to drive a Cadillac some day. Technical training is certainly essential and scholastic training is indispensable, but there must be something more than book knowledge. The communists have overcome illiteracy with reading, writing and a knowledge of subversive atheistic materialism. We must overcome illiteracy with reading and writing, but also with a knowledge of the spiritual dignity of man which raises the moral atmosphere, giving strength of character to the individual.
We in Canada need all our strength and determination, our intelligence and integrity. Our response to the challenge must be wholehearted and wholeminded. May we keep in mind what the United Nations organization is and what its agencies cover. If we are to play our part effectively and constructively we must realize the relationship between the whole and its parts, and keep in mind the various aspects of its activities.
We have made notable contributions in the field of technical assistance by providing experts to advise less developed countries. We are helping them to improve their methods of administration, production and home living. But beyond all this lies the fundamental responsibility to provide leadership for an informed and thoughtful public opinion in support of the United Nations organization's effort to eradicate illiteracy with principles of common decency and for the protection of mankind.
On motion of Mr. Tustin the debate was adjourned.
